entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11006"/><div sID="gen19829" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11006"/><hi type="bold">5. three hundred and ninety days--</hi>The three hundred ninety years of punishment appointed for Israel, and forty for Judah, cannot refer to the siege of Jerusalem. That siege is referred to in <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.1-Ezek.4.3">Eze 4:1-3</reference>, and in a sense restricted to the literal siege, but comprehending the whole train of punishment to be inflicted for their sin; therefore we read here merely of its sore pressure, not of its result. The sum of three hundred ninety and forty years is four hundred thirty, a period famous in the history of the covenant-people, being that of their sojourn in Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.40">Ex 12:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.41">41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.17">Ga 3:17</reference>). The forty alludes to the forty years in the wilderness. Elsewhere (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.68">De 28:68</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.9.3">Ho 9:3</reference>), God threatened to bring them back to Egypt, which must mean, not Egypt literally, but a bondage as bad as that one in Egypt. So now God will reduce them to a kind of new Egyptian bondage to the world: Israel, the greater transgressor, for a longer period than Judah (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.35-Ezek.20.38">Eze 20:35-38</reference>). Not the whole of the four hundred thirty years of the Egypt state is appointed to Israel; but this shortened by the forty years of the wilderness sojourn, to imply, that a way is open to their return to life by their having the Egypt state merged into that of the wilderness; that is, by ceasing from idolatry and seeking in their sifting and sore troubles, through God's covenant, a restoration to righteousness and peace [Fairbairn]. The three hundred ninety, in reference to the sin of Israel, was also literally true, being the years from the setting up of the calves by Jeroboam (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.20-1Kgs.12.33">1Ki 12:20-33</reference>), that is, from 975 to 583 B.C.: about the year of the Babylonians captivity; and perhaps the forty of Judah refers to that part of Manasseh's fifty-five years' reign in which he had not repented, and which, we are expressly told, was the cause of God's removal of Judah, notwithstanding Josiah's reformation (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.10-1Kgs.21.16">1Ki 21:10-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.26">2Ki 23:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.27">27</reference>). <div eID="gen19829" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11007"/><div sID="gen19830" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11007"/><hi type="bold">6. each day for a year--</hi>literally, "a day for a year, a day for a year." Twice repeated, to mark more distinctly the reference to <reference osisRef="Num.14.34">Nu 14:34</reference>. The picturing of the future under the image of the past, wherein the meaning was far from lying on the surface, was intended to arouse to a less superficial mode of thinking, just as the partial veiling of truth in Jesus' parables was designed to stimulate inquiry; also to remind men that God's dealings in the past are a key to the future, for He moves on the same everlasting principles, the forms alone being transitory. <div eID="gen19830" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11010"/><div sID="gen19835" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11010"/><hi type="bold">9. wheat ... barley, &c.--</hi>Instead of simple flour used for delicate cakes (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.6">Ge 18:6</reference>), the Jews should have a coarse mixture of six different kinds of grain, such as the poorest alone would eat.<div eID="gen19835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19836" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fitches--</hi>spelt or dhourra.<div eID="gen19836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">three hundred and ninety--</hi>The forty days are omitted, since these latter typify the wilderness period when Israel stood separate from the Gentiles and their pollution, though partially chastened by stint of bread and water (<reference osisRef="Ezek.4.16">Eze 4:16</reference>), whereas the eating of the polluted bread in the three hundred ninety days implies a forced residence "among the Gentiles" who were polluted with idolatry (<reference osisRef="Ezek.4.13">Eze 4:13</reference>). This last is said of "Israel" primarily, as being the most debased (<reference osisRef="Ezek.4.9-Ezek.4.15">Eze 4:9-15</reference>); they had spiritually sunk to a level with the heathen, therefore God will make their condition outwardly to correspond. Judah and Jerusalem fare less severely, being less guilty: they are to "eat bread by weight and with care," that is, have a stinted supply and be chastened with the milder discipline of the wilderness period. But Judah also is secondarily referred to in the three hundred ninety days, as having fallen, like Israel, into Gentile defilements; if, then, the Jews are to escape from the exile among Gentiles, which is their just punishment, they must submit again to the wilderness probation (<reference osisRef="Ezek.4.16">Eze 4:16</reference>). <div eID="gen19837" type="x-p"/>

Peter felt the same scruple at a similar command (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.14">Ac 10:14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.65.4">Is 65:4</reference>). Flesh of animals three days killed was prohibited ( Le 7:17 , 18 ; 19:6 , 7 ).
